Pregnancy

How to Prepare for Labor: A Third Trimester Checklist

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To prepare for labor, work in three passes from about 28 weeks: take a childbirth class and practice coping skills first, prepare your body and handle logistics between 32 and 36 weeks, then rehearse the details of the day from 36 weeks on. Spreading the work out keeps any single week light. This guide gives you a week-anchored checklist for each pass, so the day feels legible instead of looming.

Weeks 28 to 32: book a class and learn how labor works

Book a childbirth class now if you have not already. Popular classes fill up, and you want to finish by about 36 to 37 weeks so the information is fresh and the course is done before you reach full term, when labor becomes increasingly likely. Ask your provider, hospital, or local health unit what is available, and pick the format that fits your life: a multi-week evening series, a single weekend day, or a live online course. A good class walks you through the stages of labor, comfort techniques, what your support person can do, and common interventions such as monitoring and epidurals, with time to ask your own questions.

Alongside the class, learn the shape of labor at a high level so the day feels familiar instead of mysterious. Early labor is usually the longest part, with contractions that gradually get stronger, longer, and closer together, and with a first baby it can last many hours. Active labor is more intense, then comes pushing, then delivering the placenta. You do not need to memorize details. A rough map is enough to help you rest at home in early labor instead of rushing in too soon. Recognizing when labor has actually started is its own topic, and our guide to the signs of labor covers it.

Weeks 28 to 32: practice one or two coping skills

Pick one breathing pattern and start practicing it now, weeks before you need it. A simple option is a slow breath in through your nose and a longer, softer breath out through your mouth. Practice during Braxton Hicks tightenings, in the shower, or for two minutes before bed, so the pattern is automatic when a real contraction arrives. Add upright positions to your repertoire: leaning forward over a counter or the back of a chair, kneeling on hands and knees, or sitting and rocking on a birth ball. Many people find that staying upright and moving makes contractions easier to work with than lying flat.

Bring your support person into the practice. Counterpressure, which is steady firm pressure on the lower back during a contraction, and a hip squeeze, where they press inward on the sides of your hips, are two techniques a partner can learn in an evening. Rehearse them a few times so nobody is reading instructions between contractions. Keep the whole toolkit small on purpose. One breathing pattern, two positions, and one partner technique that you have actually practiced will serve you better on the day than a long list of ideas you saw once in a video and never tried with your own body.

Weeks 32 to 36: prepare your body

If your pregnancy is uncomplicated and your clinician agrees, keep moving through the third trimester. Walking, swimming, stationary cycling, and prenatal yoga or stretching all count, and mainstream guidance supports around 150 minutes of moderate activity a week in a healthy pregnancy. The goal is not fitness gains. Labor is physical work, and regular movement supports stamina, sleep, and mood in the weeks before it. Stop and contact your clinician if exercise brings on bleeding, leaking fluid, dizziness, chest pain, or regular contractions. Pelvic floor exercises matter too, and they have their own detailed guide on this site.

From about 34 to 35 weeks, you can add perineal massage if you want to. With clean hands and a little unscented oil or water-based lubricant, place one or two thumbs just inside the vaginal opening and press gently downward toward the rectum and out to the sides, holding a mild stretching feeling for a minute or two, a few times a week. Evidence suggests it may reduce the chance of tears that need stitches, particularly in a first vaginal birth. It should stretch, not hurt. Skip it and ask your clinician first if you have an infection, bleeding, placenta previa, or have been told to avoid vaginal contact.

Weeks 32 to 36: handle the logistics

Between 32 and 36 weeks, clear the practical tasks that are miserable to do in a hurry. Install the car seat and have the installation checked; many hospitals, fire stations, and community programs offer inspections by certified child passenger safety technicians, and it is common for a first installation to need adjusting. Pre-register at your hospital or birth center so the paperwork is done before you arrive in labor, and confirm what identification and insurance or health card details they want. If you have other children or pets, line up two people who could cover them, one primary and one backup, and tell them what a middle-of-the-night call might look like.

This is also the window to confirm who will support you in labor. If a partner, friend, or family member is coming, talk through what help you want and make sure they know the coping techniques you have practiced. If you are considering a doula, interview and book one now, since many take a limited number of clients per month. Share your preferences with whoever attends, and if you want them written down, our birth plan guide walks through that document step by step. Packing is covered in our hospital bag checklist. Save your support people's numbers somewhere you can find them half asleep.

Weeks 36 and beyond: rehearse the day and settle your mind

From 36 weeks, rehearse the day itself. Drive the route to your hospital or birth center at least once, note where to park, and find out which entrance is open at night. Ask your provider for their exact when-to-call rule, since practices vary, and write it down word for word along with the after-hours phone number. Then review pain relief options while you can think clearly: an epidural, nitrous oxide where it is offered, short-acting IV medicines, and unmedicated coping with movement, water, and breathing. You are not committing to anything. You are making sure that decisions during labor are informed rather than improvised, and you can change your mind at any point.

Mental preparation is mostly about trading a perfect script for informed flexibility. Labor rarely follows the plan exactly, and people tend to cope better when they expect adjustments rather than treating them as failures. Name your specific fears to someone qualified to answer them, whether that is your provider or your class instructor, because a vague dread usually shrinks when it becomes a concrete question. Keep practicing your breathing for a couple of minutes a day. Jot your questions, practice dates, and the when-to-call rule in BeMama or a notebook. And at any week, call your clinician right away for bleeding, leaking fluid, severe headache, vision changes, or a noticeable drop in your baby's movements, and go straight to emergency care for heavy bleeding or severe, constant abdominal pain.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Birth preferences are most useful as a flexible conversation about priorities, pain relief, support, newborn care, and what may change if safety concerns arise. Labor signs and the timing for hospital assessment should follow instructions from the local maternity service.

Induction and cesarean birth are clinical decisions with benefits, risks, and alternatives that depend on gestational age and the health of the pregnant person and fetus. Ask what is recommended, why, what alternatives exist, and what to expect during recovery.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to prepare questions, preferences, hospital details, and the instructions your maternity team provides. It cannot diagnose labor or determine the safest mode or timing of birth.

When to seek help

Contact maternity care for regular painful contractions as instructed, ruptured membranes, bleeding, reduced fetal movement, severe pain, or any urgent concern.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Book a childbirth class around 28 to 32 weeks so it finishes before 37 weeks.
  • Practice one breathing pattern, two upright positions, and one partner technique until they feel automatic.
  • Stay gently active, and consider perineal massage from about 34 to 35 weeks.
  • Install and check the car seat, pre-register, and confirm your support person by 36 weeks.
  • Learn your provider's exact when-to-call rule and review pain relief options before labor starts.

Frequently asked questions

When should I take childbirth classes?

Most people start a childbirth class between about 28 and 32 weeks, aiming to finish by 36 to 37 weeks. That leaves time to practice what you learn while keeping it fresh. If you are closer to your due date, a condensed one-day or online class still helps, so book whatever fits the time you have left.

How do you do perineal massage?

With clean hands and unscented oil or water-based lubricant, gently press one or two thumbs just inside the vaginal opening downward and out to the sides, holding a mild stretch for a minute or two, a few times a week from about 34 to 35 weeks. It should feel like stretching, not pain. Ask your clinician first if you have an infection, bleeding, or a condition such as placenta previa.

What exercises help prepare your body for birth?

Regular moderate activity, such as walking, swimming, and prenatal yoga, is the most useful physical preparation in most healthy pregnancies. Mainstream guidance supports around 150 minutes a week when your clinician agrees. Upright positions and gentle stretching you practice now also double as coping tools during labor. No specific exercise guarantees a shorter or easier birth, so aim for consistency rather than intensity.

How can I prepare for labor mentally?

Prepare mentally by learning the stages of labor, practicing one or two coping skills until they feel automatic, and reviewing pain relief options before the day arrives. Expect the plan to flex, since labor rarely follows a script exactly. Naming specific fears to your provider or class instructor turns vague dread into questions that can actually be answered.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
